subject: computer-science
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Primary memory (RAM, ROM and virtual memory)
Secondary storage types and their characteristics
Data representation (binary, hex, images, sound) and compression

questions.q: What does the abbreviation RAM stand for?
options: Random Access Memory
Read Access Memory
Rapid Application Memory
Random Allocation Memory
questions.explain: RAM stands for Random Access Memory, the computer's main volatile working memory.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes RAM?
options: It is volatile and loses its contents when power is removed
It is non-volatile and keeps its contents when power is removed
It can only be read from, not written to
It permanently stores the boot-up instructions
questions.explain: RAM is volatile, so any data it holds is lost once the computer is switched off.

questions.q: Which characteristic best describes ROM?
options: Non-volatile and normally read-only
Volatile and freely read/write
Used to temporarily hold running programs
An area of the hard disk used as extra memory
questions.explain: ROM is non-volatile read-only memory that typically stores the boot/start-up instructions.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of virtual memory?
options: To use part of secondary storage as an extension of RAM when RAM is full
To store the boot-up program permanently
To speed up the CPU's clock
To store data that must survive a power cut in RAM
questions.explain: Virtual memory moves data to secondary storage to free up RAM when physical memory is insufficient.

questions.q: Why can using virtual memory slow a computer down?
options: Secondary storage is much slower to access than RAM
Virtual memory reduces the amount of ROM available
It increases the CPU clock speed too far
It permanently deletes data from RAM
questions.explain: Reading and writing to secondary storage is far slower than RAM, so heavy use of virtual memory reduces performance.

questions.q: A user notices that opening many programs at once makes their computer sluggish. Adding what would most directly help?
options: More RAM
More ROM
A faster optical drive
A larger monitor
questions.explain: More RAM allows more programs and data to be held in fast primary memory, reducing reliance on slow virtual memory.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of optical storage?
options: Blu-ray disc
Solid state drive
Magnetic tape
USB flash drive
questions.explain: Optical storage such as CD, DVD and Blu-ray uses a laser to read and write data.

questions.q: Which technology does a solid state drive (SSD) use to store data?
options: Flash memory with no moving parts
Spinning magnetic platters
A laser and reflective disc
Volatile RAM chips
questions.explain: SSDs use non-volatile flash memory and contain no moving parts, unlike magnetic hard disk drives.

questions.q: Which storage device is magnetic?
options: Hard disk drive (HDD)
DVD-ROM
Solid state drive
USB memory stick
questions.explain: An HDD stores data magnetically on spinning platters, making it a magnetic storage device.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of an SSD compared with an HDD of the same capacity?
options: Faster access speeds and greater durability
Always much cheaper per gigabyte
It is a volatile form of storage
It requires a laser to read data
questions.explain: With no moving parts, SSDs are faster and more shock-resistant than HDDs, though usually more costly per gigabyte.

questions.q: Why is magnetic tape often chosen for long-term archival backups of large data sets?
options: It offers very high capacity at a low cost per gigabyte
It provides the fastest random access to any file
It is volatile and cheap to refresh
It never needs a device to read it
questions.explain: Magnetic tape stores huge amounts of data cheaply, which suits archiving despite its slow serial access.

questions.q: How many bits are there in one byte?
questions.explain: One byte is made up of 8 bits.

questions.q: How many bits make up a nibble?
questions.explain: A nibble is 4 bits, which is half of a byte.

questions.q: In the OCR specification, how many bytes are in one kilobyte?
questions.explain: OCR defines the prefixes using powers of ten, so 1 kilobyte = 1000 bytes.

questions.q: Which list places the units in order from smallest to largest?
options: Bit, nibble, byte, kilobyte, megabyte
Byte, bit, nibble, kilobyte, megabyte
Nibble, bit, byte, megabyte, kilobyte
Bit, byte, nibble, kilobyte, megabyte
questions.explain: The units increase in size: 1 bit, 4 bits (nibble), 8 bits (byte), then kilobyte and megabyte.

questions.q: What is the base (radix) of the hexadecimal number system?
questions.explain: Hexadecimal is base 16, using the digits 0-9 and letters A-F.

questions.q: Why do programmers often use hexadecimal instead of long binary numbers?
options: It is shorter and easier for humans to read and less error-prone
It is the only base a computer can store
It uses fewer than two symbols
It removes the need to store data in binary at all
questions.explain: One hex digit represents four bits, so hex gives a compact, human-friendly way of writing binary values.

questions.q: What is the key difference between lossy and lossless compression?
options: Lossy permanently discards some data, whereas lossless can restore the original exactly
Lossless permanently discards data, whereas lossy restores the original exactly
Both remove data permanently in the same way
Neither reduces the size of the file
questions.explain: Lossy compression removes data to save space, while lossless retains all data so the original can be perfectly rebuilt.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of lossless compression?
options: Run length encoding (RLE)
Reducing the sample rate of audio
Lowering the colour depth of an image
Deleting every other pixel
questions.explain: Run length encoding stores repeated runs of data compactly without losing any information, so it is lossless.

questions.q: What does the colour depth of an image determine?
options: The number of different colours each pixel can be
The width and height of the image in pixels
The physical size of the screen
The frame rate of the image
questions.explain: Colour depth is the number of bits per pixel, which sets how many distinct colours a pixel can represent.

questions.q: What happens to a sound file when the sample rate is increased?
options: The quality and the file size both increase
The quality increases but the file size decreases
Both the quality and file size decrease
Neither the quality nor the file size changes
questions.explain: A higher sample rate captures the sound more accurately but records more samples, increasing the file size.

questions.q: What is the denary value of the 8-bit binary number 00101010?
What is the denary number 42 written in hexadecimal?
options: 2A
A2
questions.explain: 42 = (2 x 16) + 10, and 10 is A in hex, giving 2A.

questions.q: An image is 200 x 100 pixels with a colour depth of 3 bits. What is its file size in bits (ignoring metadata)?
options: 60000 bits
20000 bits
600 bits
30000 bits
questions.explain: File size = width x height x colour depth = 200 x 100 x 3 = 60000 bits.

questions.q: How many different colours can be represented by a colour depth of 4 bits?
questions.explain: The number of colours is 2 to the power of the colour depth, so 2^4 = 16.
